stem: A cancer detection model has 99% accuracy on a dataset where 99% of patients are healthy. This model is likely:

options.text: Excellent — 99% accuracy is near-perfect
Useless — it probably predicts 'healthy' for everyone and misses all cancer cases
Overfitting to the training data
Underfitting — it needs more training

explanation_after: On a dataset that's 99% healthy, a model that always predicts 'healthy' gets 99% accuracy without detecting a single cancer. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets — use precision/recall instead.

options.text: True Positives / (True Positives + False Positives)
True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives)
True Negatives / (True Negatives + False Positives)
Correct predictions / Total predictions

explanation_after: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). It measures 'of all actual positives, how many did I correctly identify?' High recall means few positives are missed.

stem: For a medical diagnosis model, why is recall (sensitivity) usually more important than precision?

options.text: Because medical models are trained on large datasets
Because missing a positive case (false negative) is more dangerous than a false alarm
Because precision is harder to compute
Because medical datasets are always balanced

explanation_after: A false negative (telling a sick patient they're healthy) can be life-threatening. A false positive (unnecessary follow-up test) is inconvenient but manageable. High recall ensures sick patients aren't missed.

stem: What does a ROC AUC of 0.5 mean?

options.text: The model is 50% accurate
The model performs no better than random guessing
The model has 50% recall
Half the predictions are correct

explanation_after: AUC = 0.5 means the model performs equivalently to random guessing. AUC = 1.0 is perfect. AUC < 0.5 means the model is worse than random (often indicating inverted labels).

stem: 5-fold cross-validation provides more reliable evaluation than a single train/test split because:

options.text: It uses more total data
Each example appears in the test fold exactly once, giving a less variance-dependent estimate
It's faster to compute
It removes the need for a test set

explanation_after: With 5-fold CV, every example is tested exactly once across 5 different train/test splits. The average metric is more stable than a single split, which might be unusually easy or hard by chance.

stem: F1 score is used instead of accuracy when:

options.text: You want a single metric that balances precision and recall, especially for imbalanced classes
Accuracy computation is too slow
You have more than two classes
Your model is a neural network

explanation_after: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It's preferred when classes are imbalanced or when both false positives and false negatives matter — where accuracy can be misleading.

stem: Unlike a medical diagnosis model, a spam filter that occasionally misses a spam email (a false negative) is far less costly than one that sends a legitimate email to the spam folder (a false positive). This means a spam filter should typically be tuned to prioritise:

options.text: Recall over precision, exactly like the medical diagnosis case
Precision over recall — minimising false positives even if it lets more spam through
ROC AUC over F1 score
Training accuracy over validation accuracy

explanation_after: The right precision/recall balance depends on which error type costs more. In medical diagnosis, missing a real case (false negative) is worse, so recall is prioritised. For spam filtering, hiding a real email (false positive) is usually more disruptive than letting an occasional spam email through, so precision is prioritised instead — the opposite tradeoff from the medical example.

stem: On a highly imbalanced fraud-detection dataset (0.1% fraud), a model reports an impressive ROC AUC of 0.95. Why might this metric still be misleading?

options.text: ROC AUC can never legitimately exceed 0.9, so 0.95 must indicate a bug

ROC AUC's false-positive rate is calculated over the huge negative class, which stays low almost by default, so AUC can look strong even if the model misses most actual fraud; Precision-Recall AUC is often more informative here
ROC AUC is only mathematically defined for perfectly balanced datasets
A high ROC AUC guarantees high recall for the minority class

explanation_after: ROC AUC depends on the false-positive rate, which is computed over the (enormous) negative class, so it naturally stays low and keeps AUC looking strong even when many actual frauds are missed. On heavily imbalanced problems, Precision-Recall AUC — which focuses on how well the model finds the rare positive class — gives a more honest picture of performance.
